questions.stem: Two supplementary angles are in the ratio 7:3. What is the measure of the larger angle?

options.option_text: 54° (smaller angle — three parts of 18° each)
108° (from a 6:4 ratio misread, six parts of 18°)
126° (seven parts of 18°, the larger supplementary angle)
144° (from treating ratio as 8:2 and taking eight parts)

questions.explanation: C is correct. Total parts = 7 + 3 = 10. Supplementary angles sum = 180°, so each part = 180°/10 = 18°. Larger angle = 7 × 18° = 126°. Verify: 126° + 54° = 180° ✓, ratio 126:54 = 7:3 ✓. Option A (54°) is the smaller angle — a classic reversal trap. **Short Trick:** Larger angle = 7/(7+3) × 180° = 7/10 × 180° = 126°.

questions.stem: An exterior angle of a triangle measures 130°. One of the two non-adjacent interior angles is 55°. What is the other non-adjacent interior angle?

options.option_text: 45° (subtracting 85° from 130° due to a step error)
55° (copying the given non-adjacent interior angle value)
75° (exterior angle equals sum of two remote interior angles)
95° (adding the given angle to 130° and halving incorrectly)

questions.explanation: C is correct. Exterior Angle Theorem: an exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent (remote) interior angles. So 130° = 55° + x → x = 75°. Option D (95°) is a common mistake where students add rather than subtract. Option A (45°) comes from computing the adjacent interior angle first (180° − 130° = 50°) and then subtracting incorrectly. **Short Trick:** Remote interior angle = exterior angle − given remote interior = 130° − 55° = 75°.

questions.stem: A straight line is divided at a point into two angles in the ratio 2:3. What is the measure of the smaller angle?

options.option_text: 60° (taking one-third of 180°, as if the ratio were 1:2)
72° (two-fifths of 180°, correctly applying the 2:3 ratio)
108° (the larger part, three-fifths of 180°)
120° (two-thirds of 180°, misreading ratio as 2:1)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Angles on a straight line sum to 180°. Total ratio parts = 2 + 3 = 5. Smaller angle = 2/5 × 180° = 72°. Option C (108°) is the larger angle — a reversal error. Option A (60°) comes from dividing 180° by 3 (treating as a 1:2 ratio). **Short Trick:** Smaller = (smaller ratio / total ratio) × 180° = 2/5 × 180° = 72°.

questions.stem: Two straight lines intersect at point O. One of the four angles formed is 3 times its adjacent angle. What is the larger angle?

options.option_text: 45° (the smaller adjacent angle, one-fourth of 180°)
90° (the result if both adjacent angles were assumed equal)
120° (from applying a 1:2 ratio instead of 1:3)
135° (three times the smaller, correctly solving x + 3x = 180°)

questions.explanation: D is correct. Adjacent angles at an intersection are supplementary. Let smaller angle = x; larger = 3x. So x + 3x = 180° → 4x = 180° → x = 45°. Larger = 3 × 45° = 135°. Vertically opposite angles confirm: two 45° angles and two 135° angles at the intersection. **Short Trick:** Larger angle = 3/(1+3) × 180° = 3/4 × 180° = 135°.

questions.stem: AB ∥ CD. A transversal cuts AB at P and CD at Q such that ∠APQ = (3x + 5)° and ∠PQD = (x + 35)°. What is the value of ∠APQ?

options.option_text: 35° (using x = 10 but computing only the constant terms)
50° (alternate interior angles equal; correctly solving x = 15)
65° (treating the two angles as supplementary and solving)
110° (co-interior sum error: setting 3x+5+x+35 = 180°)

questions.explanation: B is correct. ∠APQ and ∠PQD are alternate interior angles (AB ∥ CD), so they are equal. 3x + 5 = x + 35 → 2x = 30 → x = 15. ∠APQ = 3(15) + 5 = 50°. Verify: ∠PQD = 15 + 35 = 50° ✓. Option D arises from mistakenly treating them as co-interior (same-side) and summing to 180°: this gives x = 35, ∠APQ = 110°. **Short Trick:** Alternate interior angles: set equal, solve for x, then substitute.

questions.stem: PQ ∥ RS. A transversal cuts PQ at A and RS at B. The bisector of ∠QAB and the bisector of ∠ABR meet at a point T. What is ∠ATB?

options.option_text: 60° (assuming bisectors of parallel-line angles meet at 60°)
75° (partial application of co-interior sum gives 150°, halved gives 75°)
90° (bisectors of co-interior angles always meet at a right angle)
120° (from treating the full co-interior sum as the angle at T)

questions.explanation: C is correct. ∠QAB and ∠ABR are co-interior (same-side interior) angles, so ∠QAB + ∠ABR = 180°. In triangle ATB: ∠TAB = ∠QAB/2 and ∠TBA = ∠ABR/2. ∠ATB = 180° − (∠QAB/2 + ∠ABR/2) = 180° − (∠QAB + ∠ABR)/2 = 180° − 180°/2 = 90°. This result holds for any pair of co-interior angles — the bisectors always meet at 90°. **Short Trick:** Bisectors of co-interior angles → right angle. Bisectors of alternate interior angles → parallel to each other.

questions.stem: AB ∥ CD. Point O lies between the two parallel lines. Ray OA₁ meets AB making an angle of 55° with AB, and ray OC₁ meets CD making an angle of 70° with CD (both rays on the same side of O). What is ∠A₁OC₁?

options.option_text: 55° (using only the angle the ray makes with AB, ignoring CD)
70° (using only the angle the ray makes with CD, ignoring AB)
125° (sum of alternate interior angles via a parallel drawn through O)
115° (subtracting one angle from 180° and adding the other incorrectly)

questions.explanation: C is correct. Draw line EF through O parallel to both AB and CD. Since AB ∥ EF: alternate interior angle at O with ray OA₁ = 55°. Since EF ∥ CD: alternate interior angle at O with ray OC₁ = 70°. These two angles are on opposite sides of EF at O, so ∠A₁OC₁ = 55° + 70° = 125°. Crucially, the position of O between the parallels does not affect the result. **Short Trick:** ∠A₁OC₁ = (angle with AB) + (angle with CD) when rays go to opposite parallel lines.

questions.stem: In △PQR, side QR is extended to S. If ∠QPR = 45° and ∠PRS = 110°, what is ∠PQR?

options.option_text: 55° (subtracting ∠QPR from ∠PRS without applying the exterior angle theorem)
65° (exterior angle = sum of remote interiors; 110° − 45° = 65°)
70° (180° − 110° = 70°, the adjacent interior angle at R)
25° (180° − 110° − 45° = 25°, treating ∠PRS as an interior angle)

questions.explanation: B is correct. ∠PRS is an exterior angle at R (since QR is extended to S). By the Exterior Angle Theorem, ∠PRS = ∠QPR + ∠PQR. So 110° = 45° + ∠PQR → ∠PQR = 65°. Option C (70°) is the interior angle ∠PRQ = 180° − 110° = 70°, not ∠PQR. Option D (25°) wrongly treats the exterior angle as a third interior angle. Verify: ∠PQR + ∠QPR + ∠PRQ = 65° + 45° + 70° = 180° ✓.

questions.stem: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. A pair of co-interior angles is in the ratio 5:4. What is the value of the larger co-interior angle?

options.option_text: 80° (smaller co-interior angle, four-ninths of 180°)
90° (equal-angle assumption, treating ratio as 1:1)
100° (larger co-interior angle, five-ninths of 180°)
120° (from treating ratio as 5:3 and taking five-eighths of 180°)

questions.explanation: C is correct. Co-interior angles sum = 180°. Total parts = 5 + 4 = 9. Each part = 180°/9 = 20°. Larger angle = 5 × 20° = 100°. Verify: 100° + 80° = 180° ✓, ratio = 100:80 = 5:4 ✓. Option A (80°) is the smaller angle. **Short Trick:** Larger = 5/9 × 180° = 100°.

questions.stem: AB ∥ CD ∥ EF. A transversal cuts AB at P, CD at Q, and EF at R. If ∠APQ = 65°, what is ∠QRF?

options.option_text: 65° (alternate interior angles between AB and EF are equal)
115° (co-interior angle of ∠APQ with EF, summing to 180°)
130° (double of 65°, incorrectly adding the angle at Q)
50° (applying an arbitrary reduction for the extra parallel line)

questions.explanation: A is correct. Since AB ∥ CD ∥ EF, all three lines are parallel. ∠APQ is the angle on the A-side above AB (alternate interior side). ∠QRF is the angle on the F-side below EF, on the opposite side of the transversal. These are alternate interior angles with respect to the outermost pair of parallel lines AB and EF, so ∠QRF = ∠APQ = 65°. CD being between them does not change this — transitivity of parallel lines applies. Option B (115°) would be the co-interior angle, which is on the same side.

questions.stem: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2:3:4. One side is extended to form an exterior angle adjacent to the largest interior angle. What is the measure of this exterior angle?

options.option_text: 80° (the largest interior angle itself, not the exterior angle)
100° (180° minus the largest interior angle of 80°)
120° (exterior angle of the medium angle, 180° minus 60°)
140° (exterior angle of the smallest angle, 180° minus 40°)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Total ratio parts = 2 + 3 + 4 = 9. Each part = 180°/9 = 20°. Interior angles: 40°, 60°, 80°. Largest interior angle = 4 × 20° = 80°. Exterior angle adjacent to it = 180° − 80° = 100°. Also verifiable via Exterior Angle Theorem: exterior at C = ∠A + ∠B = 40° + 60° = 100° ✓. Option C (120°) is the exterior of the middle angle; Option D (140°) is the exterior of the smallest. **Short Trick:** Largest interior = 4/9 × 180° = 80°; exterior = 100°.

questions.stem: AB ∥ CD. A transversal meets AB at P and CD at Q. The angle bisector of ∠BPQ makes an angle of 35° with AB. What is ∠PQC?

options.option_text: 35° (treating bisected angle as the co-interior pair directly)
70° (the full ∠BPQ before bisection, which equals its alternate interior angle)
110° (co-interior partner of ∠BPQ)
145° (treating 35° as co-interior to ∠PQC instead of ∠BPQ)

questions.explanation: B is correct. The bisector of ∠BPQ makes 35° with AB, so ∠BPQ = 2 × 35° = 70°. ∠PQC and ∠BPQ are alternate interior angles (AB ∥ CD), so ∠PQC = ∠BPQ = 70°. Option C (110°) is the co-interior partner: ∠PQD = 180° − 70° = 110°, but ∠PQC is on the C-side (alternate, not co-interior). **Short Trick:** Angle before bisection = 2 × (angle with bisector). Alternate interior angle = same value.

questions.stem: Two parallel lines l and m are cut by a transversal n. On the same side of n, the interior angles are (5x + 10)° and (7x − 10)°. Find x.

options.option_text: 10 (from setting the two angles equal — alternate interior error)
15 (correct — co-interior angles sum to 180°, giving 12x = 180)
20 (from 7x − 10 = 180° alone, ignoring the other angle)
25 (from 5x + 10 = 180° alone, ignoring the other angle)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Co-interior (same-side interior) angles sum to 180°. (5x + 10) + (7x − 10) = 180 → 12x = 180 → x = 15. Verify: angles = 5(15)+10 = 85° and 7(15)−10 = 95°. Sum = 180° ✓. Option A (x = 10) comes from setting the angles equal — this would be correct for alternate interior angles, not co-interior. **Short Trick:** Same side = supplementary → set sum = 180°. Opposite sides = alternate → set equal.

questions.stem: Rays OA, OB, OC are drawn from a common point O such that ∠AOB = 80°, ∠BOC = 40°, and ∠AOC is a reflex angle. What is the reflex angle ∠AOC?

options.option_text: 120° (sum of ∠AOB + ∠BOC, treating the acute path as ∠AOC)
240° (360° − 120°, the reflex version of the acute ∠AOC)
280° (360° − 80°, ignoring ∠BOC entirely)
320° (360° − 40°, ignoring ∠AOB entirely)

questions.explanation: B is correct. The acute ∠AOC = ∠AOB + ∠BOC = 80° + 40° = 120° (assuming OB lies between OA and OC in the acute region). Reflex ∠AOC = 360° − 120° = 240°. Option A (120°) is the acute angle, not the reflex. Options C and D arise from ignoring one of the rays. Note: always check which of the two angles formed by OA and OC is reflex (> 180°). **Short Trick:** Reflex angle = 360° − (non-reflex angle).
